utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Doyle, let's just continue with the meeting we were discussing, the one that was held in my office, since Mr. May adjourned the session. Towards the very end, what you wrote here is the following, and I'll read it out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Wait a moment. Let's just make sure we've all got the tab. It's tab 12. The witness should have it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had assumed that he had it, because that's where we broke off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's make sure that he has it. Colm Doyle, have you got it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [In English] "There was no alternative to the EC peace conference for working out a solution to the crisis in Bosnia-Herzegovina. It was impossible for anyone to emerge as a winner from war in the republic and there were no innocent parties. Bosnia-Herzegovina was a state of three equal peoples and" -- [Interpretation] Three equitable peoples. "[In English] Any argument based -- any agreement" -- [Interpretation] I assume that this is supposed to be "agreement" rather than "argument."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] The third paragraph, penultimate paragraph.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Presiding Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: "Because the international community had been ill-advised to recognise Bosnia-Herzegovina when it did, but Belgrade was doing politically everything it could to bring about peace. It was obvious in its interest to do so. Whereas, for the Muslim Izetbegovic was refusing to negotiate and seemed inclined to continue the civil war. Belgrade would take any concrete steps required of it to promote a settlement." [Interpretation] Further on there is what you added in hand, but even a person from elementary school in Yugoslavia would not say a thing like that, that Sarajevo is a Muslim town. Everybody knew that Sarajevo was a multi-ethnic town, Mr. Doyle. But I mentioned here that Izetbegovic rejected negotiations and wanted to continue the war. What I'm asking you now is -- I have this in front of me. Let me just take a look. Let's just be quite clear on this, Mr. May. I am not exhibiting this statement. I'm asking Mr. Doyle, because he is mentioned here, is this right. In the statement made by General MacKenzie, which was provided here - I have the page in front of me, ERN 0011 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch the exact number.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It says - do you recall this? - "The 23rd of April, Philip Morillon and I met with Lord Carrington and the special envoy of the European Community, Colm Doyle. We said to them that we thought that the Bosnian Presidency decided to compel the international community to act militarily and that therefore they were not prepared to observe the cease-fire. President Izetbegovic presented the position that Bosnia was an internationally recognised country and that the world should save it from its Serb enemies." Do you recall that, Mr. Doyle?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not recall that at all. I recall the comments that you passed in relation to the meeting I had with you in your office. Anything outside of that, I don't have any detailed knowledge of.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So MacKenzie says that he met up with you and with Carrington and that he and Morillon said to you that the Muslim side actually does not want to have a cease-fire effected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You read that and the witness doesn't remember it, so there's no point reading it again.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I just wish to point out that what they said to them then coincides with the assessment I made in the talks, that the Muslims did not really want a cease-fire and that they kept imposing a continuation of the civil war, whereas the Serb leadership in Pale showed that they did want a cease-fire and that they did want a political solution. I assume that you were aware of that, Mr. Doyle.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I feel I can say here is that I'm attempting to accurately reflect the comments that were passed to you -- to me by you when we had a meeting in your office, Mr. Milosevic. And that's all I can say. Whether they were put into practice is quite another matter, but my function in that meeting on the instructions I got from London was that I should go and meet you in your office because it was at your request, I should listen to what you wanted to say because we assumed that you'd want to say to me and what you wanted the European -- or the peace conference to hear. And I tried to do that in a professional manner as I could.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Yesterday, you gave evidence about these events that related to the keeping of Izetbegovic after he returned from Lisbon. I would like you to confirm or deny what General MacKenzie says about this on the same page that I quoted to you a minute ago, because he was also a participant in these events. I assume that you remember that. Is that right, Mr. Doyle?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume, Mr. Milosevic, you're referring to the day the president was returning from talks in Lisbon?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is what General MacKenzie says and you tell me whether he presented things accurately or not. It is my impression that your approach is somewhat different. "On the 3rd of May, in the morning, Ejub Ganic, vice-president, came to my office and met with me and Colm Doyle." So Ganic met with you and MacKenzie. "Ganic explained that President Izetbegovic had been kidnapped at Sarajevo airport upon returning from Lisbon and that the JNA was keeping him in custody in the Lukavica Barracks, Lukavica. Ganic said that he was not a strong leader and that he needed his president so that he would keep the radical leaders of the Bosnian Territorial Defence under his control."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Pause there. Just pause there and let the witness comment, if he can, upon what has been put to him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I agree that on the 3rd of May I was with General MacKenzie as we attempted to negotiate, and a hostage release of President Izetbegovic and the exchange with General Kukanjac and that was negotiated in the office of General MacKenzie, in the presence of Deputy President Ejub Ganic and General Aksentijevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So Ganic said that he was not a strong leader and that he needed his president in order to keep under his control the radical leaders of the Bosnian Territorial Defence who were getting out of control rapidly. Do you remember that? And General MacKenzie moves on to say the TO forces --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Wait a moment. Let the witness answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My recollection of that comment by Mr. Ganic was that by virtue of the fact that he was only one single member of the Presidency, he could not make any agreement in relation to the hostage release unless it was sanctioned by the president himself. The reference to the radical Muslims, I am not aware of. He may have said it, but I'm not aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you do not recall that, what General MacKenzie says. Do you remember the rest what he says? "I went with Colm Doyle," that is to say, with you, "to the Lukavica Barracks and that's where I found the president Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. with his daughter and bodyguards." At the moment when I arrived, President Izetbegovic was talking on the telephone with General Kukanjac. He told me that General Kukanjac agreed to have an exchange of the two of us. "Will you organise this for us?" Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The portion that I remember is that I accompanied General MacKenzie when both of us in an armoured car went to Lukavica Barracks. When we arrived inside the barracks, General MacKenzie himself went in to meet the president. I remained on the outside for approximately two hours, after which time General MacKenzie asked me to enter and meet the president and attempt to persuade him to carry out the exchange as we had originally agreed upon. But I was not in the office when General MacKenzie met the president on that morning. I was outside and there is television footage to that extent available.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Doyle. Is it well known that the Territorial Defence forces, that is to say, the Muslim forces, held under siege the headquarters of General Kukanjac in the eastern part of town? Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General MacKenzie says that later an evacuation was agreed, the evacuation of General Kukanjac and his entire staff, numbering 400 persons, as an exchange for releasing the president. It was agreed that Colm Doyle would remain in Lukavica with the bodyguards and that I bring the president and his daughter and that we arrange the exchange in that way. Is that the way it was?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And now, the events that I imagine you are aware of. You had the opportunity of knowing about all of this. "General MacKenzie said that we set out for Sarajevo on a convoy. When we reached a hill from which Sarajevo can be seen on the southern side, we could see that the town was indeed a site of heavy fighting. As we were getting closer to the centre of town, we came across numerous destroyed tanks and personnel carriers, armoured personnel carriers. We saw the corpses of people. I never saw such a picturesque condemnation of the folly of war. After we arrived in the headquarters of General Kukanjac, the preparations for evacuation were made official. When the set time came up, all of a sudden I received information that Ganic had called our headquarters to say that the agreement was called off. The president confirmed that we should go on and we set out with the president and his daughter in one of our own APCs. Soon after our departure, our convoy was ambushed by the Territorial Defence during a brief skirmish, seven or eight JNA officers were killed in cold blood. The Territorial Defence --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness cannot begin to comment upon all this unless he's given a chance to do so. Colonel, can you assist us with what the accused has been reading out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can, Your Honour. I would like to say here that as Mr. Milosevic has himself said, that when the decision was made to move the president, I remained in Lukavica. I was not a voluntary person who remained. I was held to a certain extent as collateral against anything happening. This came about because when we had negotiated the release of the president and we went to move the president, the senior military officer in Lukavica turned around to me and said, "You have only negotiated the release of the president. That does not include his daughter or his security people." I strenuously objected to this and a compromise was reached whereby I agreed that I would stay in Lukavica. So all of the events that took place subsequent to that in relation to the convoy, I was not a witness to. I saw coverage on television. I know that some of the reports coming back to Lukavica were extraordinarily exaggerated by JNA officers because I was taken out and a pistol was put to my head by the senior military officer. I fortunately was in communication with a member of the European Community Monitoring Mission through a held -- a hand-held phone which I have, and he told me that there were wild exaggerations as to what was happening. However, I do agree with Mr. Milosevic when he said that there was an ambush on the convoy, that some JNA officers were shot, and that some members of the JNA were taken captive. My function at the end of this was attempt to ensure that the agreement was carried out by doing everything I could to ensure that those soldiers were subsequently released, which occurred. But I am not in the position here to give a definitive definition on exactly what happened on that convoy, because I at that stage was being held at Lukavica Barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You say that you heard that some officers had been arrested, MacKenzie say that is six or seven officers of the JNA were killed in cold blood, and about 200 soldiers were taken captive that's what MacKenzie says. That is what MacKenzie wrote. That is a well-known thing. I imagine that you had to have been aware of this?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've just said that I agree with that, that there were JNA officers killed and there was an ambush and soldiers were taken captive. So we are not in dispute on this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Is this correct, what General MacKenzie says: "On the 5th of May --" he is talking about Marrack Goulding's arrival, the deputy -- secretary-general for special political affairs about his arrival in Pale?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: And he says, "The European Community refused to include the Bosnian Serbs in their cease-fire negotiations. For them perhaps it had a diplomatic purpose, but it seemed ridiculous for the ordinary soldier not to have one of the main parties to the conflict included in the cease-fire negotiations. My question, Mr. Doyle, is: Why did you exclude the Bosnian Serbs from the cease-fire negotiations? Why did you have such a discriminatory attitude towards them, in view of everything that was going on?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The agreement was -- that was to be negotiated was that when the president was released and General Kukanjac had the cordon lifted from around the barracks, that the president and the general would be brought to the PTT building, which was now the headquarters of the United Nations in Sarajevo, and there I would chair negotiations for a continued cease-fire. After the events of the convoy, this changed, so I arranged a meeting of all parties in the UN headquarters in order to negotiate a cease-fire. The Serb delegation did not come to the PTT building because they said they would not be safe, so I continued with the negotiations with all the parties that were available to travel and they included Mr. Abdic, Stjepan Kljujic, General Aksentijevic, the monitor mission and members of the United Nations. And there was no occasion at that time in Sarajevo that the Serb leadership would come to the PTT building.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not talking about the technical aspect of this, Mr. Doyle. I am talking about General MacKenzie's assertion that the European Community refused to include the Bosnian Serbs in their cease-fire negotiations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let that be -- let that be put to the witness so he can answer it. What is put by the accused is that the European Community refused to include the Bosnian Serbs in the cease-fire negotiations. Now, I think you've explained how that came about, but since that's put, that the Community refused to include the Bosnian Serbs, is that right or not, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, it is not correct. May I just add here that I was a representative of the peace conference, not the European Community. But there was no blank refusal by anybody to attend. We were informed that the Bosnian Serbs could not come because they were worried about their safety and their security. At this stage, Sarajevo was a dangerous place.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, just a small correction, in view of what you said just now. It's not that I am claiming that. I quoted General MacKenzie. And it says here verbatim that the European Community refused to include --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We have -- we have the point. But what he says in his Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. statement, as you know, isn't evidence, and you're putting it to the witness. But let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, you are saying that what Mr. General MacKenzie said here is not correct. Did I understand you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's a comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about this, Mr. Doyle? General MacKenzie speaks about the 6th of May. "I spent the day with Mr. Goulding. All that morning I reported to him, and in the afternoon we went on a tour of the city with President Izetbegovic. We were exposed to moderate fire. In the midst of all the Muslim town. There were strong indications that it was only a show staged for representatives of the media who were among our entourage in order to present Serbs in a bad light. Fire came from infantry weapons from the distance of 75 metres away from us within territory under Bosnian control. At the end of the activities of the day, Goulding held a press conference. We were feeling that it was very important to condemn the Territorial Defence's attack on the JNA convoy." Do you remember this and this whole show staged in order to condemn the Serbs that was made in the Muslim part of town? And as General MacKenzie says, that it was all organised for the benefit of the representatives of the media? And do you know anything at all about this practice of stage management by the Muslim forces for the benefit of the media and of the European Community?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: My diary reflects that I was all day on the 6th of May, the 7th of May, and the 8th of May, based in the PTT building attempting to negotiate the withdrawal of the federal army from all of Yugoslavia. What was happening in the city, I had no knowledge of.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. So in certain matters you limit your evidence only to what you saw with your own eyes, and in other matters you explain the entire situation, whereas you served as chief of the monitoring mission in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's not a proper question. I don't understand the basis of this criticism. What do you mean? What are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am referring to the fact that it is logical to expect of the chief of the monitoring mission to have information, because the monitoring mission covered the entire Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us ask the witness about that. Although you were in the PTT building that day, Colonel, did you have any information as to what was happening outside, particularly the -- this alleged attack which the witness -- the accused is referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just a correction here to Mr. Milosevic. At that time, I was not the head of the European Community Monitoring Mission. I was working on my own as the personal representative to Lord Carrington. But I do know that on that day in question I was aware of the fact that General MacKenzie was accompanying the president downtown Sarajevo. Apart from that, I'm not aware of what was happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: If you say so, Mr. Doyle. Is this true? "After several days, that is, on the 11th of May," says the statement of General MacKenzie, the 11th of May, page 0112194, "the European Community has been conducting marathon negotiations for several days trying to exclude Bosnian Serbs from the castle, and therefore they became less and less popular among them. In the meantime, Bosnian Serbs, led by Dr. Radovan Karadzic, were becoming more and more independent of the JNA. There were even reports about Bosnian Serb attacks on JNA units who were trying to turn over their weapons, ammunition, and equipment in exchange for a safe exit from Bosnia." Do you know anything about that, about this claim of General MacKenzie?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no knowledge of that claim by General MacKenzie, and I certainly was not aware of the comment that you've passed, that we were trying to exclude the Bosnian Serbs, because that in my view is totally incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. He says that you continued to exclude them from negotiations, and in the next passage he says, "In the afternoon, we were visited by the representative of the European Community, Colm Doyle, who came together with Mr. Santos. Colm informed us that Bosnian Serbs were a threat to the lives of his colleagues and their negotiations were leading nowhere." Therefore, General MacKenzie also says that you were excluding Serbs from negotiations and that you told them that negotiating with Bosnian Serbs was leading nowhere and that they were a threat to human lives. Is that correct, Mr. Doyle, or not?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I have no knowledge whatsoever of that statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I have to skip a number of questions. Mr. -- In fact, MacKenzie speaks about the blockade of Marsal Tito Barracks in the centre of Sarajevo and says, "Forces of the Bosnian TO held under blockade this barracks for months. Every time a sniper killed somebody inside the barracks, Serbs would respond with artillery fire from the base in Lukavica. Thus they were responding to the killings executed by Muslim forces holding the barracks under siege; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first time I've heard any reference to the fact that the -- this barracks was under siege for months. That's an impossibility. I had been in that barracks some weeks before the siege took place, so certainly the question of it being besieged by months, my recollection is that the barracks was possibly besieged -- and when I say "besieged," I mean surrounded, where nobody could leave or nobody enter. It was my understanding that that took place for approximately two days. Generally, whatever else General MacKenzie says may be his opinion. I'm not in a position to verify, because he was working with the United Nations and I was working with the peace conference. So I have really no comment on what General MacKenzie may have said, because I'm not in a position to verify his comments or otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you have no idea that they were reacting to killings executed by snipers, by forces who were surrounding the barracks. This is what General MacKenzie talks about. And you know nothing about it?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I can say at this stage is that I was very well aware that there was conflict occurring in the city of Sarajevo, which takes all sorts of sides to be involved. The exact details of individual incidents, I'm not able to comment upon. But as a military person, I am aware that in a situation of conflict, all sides take part.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How about this claim of General MacKenzie: "Serbs were outnumbered" - that's what General MacKenzie says - "by the less well-trained forces, infantry forces of the Territorial Defence, Muslim forces. However, they were anxious that they would be overrun by Muslim forces and chose to fight them from a distance." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no knowledge of it and I have no remark to make on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I will not ask you anything about the meeting between Nambiar and MacKenzie, because I see that you did not attend. MacKenzie says that "TO forces, just as the Serbs, represented an obstacle to the attainment of this goal of stopping the bloodshed." Was this also an impression that you shared?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I was sufficiently long enough in the city and having worked there to know that that could be said for any side, as long as conflict was going on, as long as people were being killed, the objective -- or my objective, as the representative of the peace conference, was to try and negotiate cease-fires so that the killing would stop. Who did what, who attained what, I really don't have much comment upon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You have no comment on this. Is MacKenzie correct on this? "There was no doubt that it was a general exchange of fire." Was that an impression that you shared?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand that question. I don't understand, "there is no doubt that it was a general exchange of fire." Could you elaborate on Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. that, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, General MacKenzie says that "The 40-hour cease-fire broke down on the 17th of June," and then he speaks about the monitoring, about John Wilson, the monitors who were on the roof of their building in order to verify who is shooting, where from, et cetera. "Both sides seldom admitted that their troops executed any action, and in rare occasions when they did admit, they said they were provoked. Artillery had caused large fires in the old part of the town. Every couple of seconds I could hear explosions. So there was no doubt that it was an all-out exchange of fire." Here I've read to you an entire passage from General MacKenzie's statement. Was there any doubt in the sense that maybe Serbs had attacked the Muslims, as you claim, or was this really, as it says here, a conflict provoked by the Muslims, as we established, beginning with the murder in the centre of Sarajevo, followed by a series of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Stop. We've established nothing. No doubt we'll be able to determine the evidence in due course. But you can't make that sort of generalisation. Now, what's the next question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may just mention here that when Mr. Milosevic refers to the 17th of June and that the monitors were in the building, the entire team of the -- of the European Community Monitor Mission were withdrawn from Sarajevo on the 12th of June and redeployed to Split in Croatia. I was evacuated from the city of Sarajevo on the 12th of June to Belgrade and then within 24 hours I was in London. So when you refer to the 17th of June, I was not in the country, nor were any of the monitors. They could have been United Nations military observers and the question of the United Nations was not within my remit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. But we have gone through in great detail this event that happened in the night between the 2nd and 3rd of May, the attack on the column, the gunfire, the exchange of Izetbegovic with the help of Kukanjac and his staff. Is this statement by General Nambiar, the force commander then, correct? That is, 00966038, page number. General Nambiar says, "The shelling began mainly after the events of the 3rd of May, 1992. Before the 3rd of May, there was no shelling of Sarajevo because at that time JNA was still there. There were shootings aimed at soldiers in the city. This was the general background against which the events took place." Can we see from this, Mr. Doyle, what it was that caused the escalation of the conflict, this event, the attack on the column, the killing of people, the taking of 200 soldiers prisoner, and all the rest that was done by the extremist forces on the Muslim side? General Nambiar says it all happened after the 3rd of May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Do you have a question? Yes, Colonel, if you'd like to, if you can, respond to what the general said in his statement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't have any comment on what the general said, because I'm not party to it. But what I can say from my own experience, having been there, is that the -- there was an escalation in the conflict after the 3rd of May, because that was the date that the president was released. But it was also the date that the commander of the JNA was released, General Kukanjac. And when he returned to Lukavica, he intimated that he would deal with Sarajevo as he felt he would. And we were very well aware that he was now in a position of taking some action against the city, because he had been held captive in his own headquarters, which was very embarrassing for him. So where I agree that the conflict seemed to intensify after that incident, I am not in a position to indicate who was responsible for it being so intensified.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Doyle, who was it that attacked the army column and killed all these officers in cold blood, as General MacKenzie says, causing great bloodshed? Who captured 200 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What the witness has said is that he is not in a position to say how it was or who caused the intensification of the conflict. Now, that's what he says. And if he's not in a position to comment on it, there's no point asking him more questions about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General Nambiar goes on to say, "This entire incident involving the ambush of the JNA column on the 3rd of May, 1992 was observed by my own soldiers. What the soldiers, the troops of General Nambiar, the force commander of the UN witnessed is verifiable and true, or do you dispute that as well?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You can call General Nambiar in due course. No point asking this witness about what General Nambiar says he saw --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not asking him what General Nambiar said, but instead, quoting General Nambiar's words and I'm asking him whether that coincides with his information, his knowledge, because both he, General Nambiar, and General MacKenzie were there, unlike me, and I'm only looking at their statements --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... as you frequently do, you're arguing with the witness, trying to get him to say something which he cannot say. He cannot go beyond the evidence which he's given. There's very little point arguing him -- arguing with him for your own point of view. Now, I'd remind you that your time is limited. You've got about 20 minutes left. If you've got any other topics you want to ask him about, you better do so.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I just want to get one thing clear, Mr. Doyle: What General Nambiar says concerning the detention of Izetbegovic is a bit different from what you've said. And I would like your comment on it. He says, "When on the 2nd of May, 1992 he returned --" meaning Izetbegovic returned, "he did not inform either us or anybody else about his arrival. When he arrived, the Serbs took him away and notified Colm Doyle, the European Community negotiator, that Izetbegovic was their guest." Was that the way it was?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The arrangement that was put in place for President Izetbegovic was that when I was informed by the Presidency that he was due to come back to the city, I would request an escort from the United Nations. On the morning in question, there was heavy fighting in the city and I was very busy, and in the middle of this I received a phone call which allegedly came from the Presidency to inform me that because of the intensification of the fighting in the city, President Izetbegovic would not be returning to Sarajevo on that day. I found out subsequently that the phone call did not come from the Presidency but came from some other source who obviously wished me to ensure that there would be no UN escort for the president, because when I received the first phone call, I requested the United Nations to stand down the escort because there would be no need, as the president was not returning. I was incorrect in this. The president did return and was taken into custody at the airport, subsequently to be taken to Lukavica Barracks. I can only surmise that it was not from the Presidency I received the phone call that he would not be returning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General Nambiar says that he did not inform anyone that he was returning. That is a bit different from what you describe.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't comment on what General Nambiar says. I can only let you know what did happen, as far as I was concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Doyle. Generally speaking, concerning the role of the European Community, whose representative you were, and bearing in mind that you were part of that mission which was officially called the European Community Monitoring Mission in Yugoslavia - that was its name - do you know that the European parliament, that is an organ of the European Community, adopted on the 9th of July, 1991 a resolution on Yugoslavia not lending its support to the unilateral secessionist acts of Slovenia and Croatia? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: My interest at that stage in July 1991 was as an officer of the Irish defence forces. I was not involved in anything with the European Community, and therefore, I have no knowledge of what you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Doyle. But since you did serve on the monitoring mission in Yugoslavia, that was the name of the mission, and you were a representative of the European Community, you must have been briefed on the positions and stances of the European Community. Somebody must have briefed you regarding the European Community's position vis-a-vis the country they were sending you to. Or you were not briefed on anything at all?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received a standard operational briefing at my own headquarters on the immediate concerns that existed within the former Yugoslavia. It did not have any regard to the area that you refer to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So nobody told you anything about the stance of the European parliament adopted regarding the crisis in Yugoslavia. Were you perhaps familiar then, if you knew nothing about the stance of the European parliament, that the ministerial council and -- of the European Community supported the integrity of Yugoslavia and the European Community emphasised that a unified and democratic Yugoslavia had the best chances of harmoniously integrating with the new Europe? Do you know anything at least about the declaration of the European Community on Yugoslavia? You must have been as a representative of the European Community about to leave for that country.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was generally aware that at that time it was put out that Yugoslavia might better be served if it continued to be a federation of -- of the various republics. The exact details, I would not have been aware of. But I had a general understanding of what the situation was, but no great detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that even the council of ministers of OSCE at the meeting in Berlin in its declaration where it also expressed its support to the unity and the territorial integrity on Yugoslavia, that was in June 1991?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I am not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that even the state secretary of the US, James Baker, at the end of his visit to Yugoslavia in end June 1991 said that the USA supports democratic and unified Yugoslavia, and solutions for its future should be sought through agreement, and the US would not recognise unilateral acts of secession? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware of the statement of James Baker.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know anything about the statements of Carrington, Cyrus Vance, and a number of other politicians who spoke about the fact that a premature recognition of these republics in fact caused the failure of the peace process in Yugoslavia? In fact, peace itself, because peace existed before that.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware of the fact that Lord Carrington expressed his view as chairman of the international peace conference that a premature recognition of the republics would not help the situation that he was trying to deal with in Bosnia. Beyond that, I only have a general knowledge, but no detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As you're aware of all these things and you're aware of all these positions of the European Community, the OSCE, the United States, et cetera, what explanation would you -- were you given as the head of mission regarding the entirely opposite acts, that is, the recognition and the treatment given to the Yugoslav crisis? Were you given any explanation for that?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't given any explanation, nor did I seek any.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree that it was rather hypocritical on the one side to support the unity of a country and its integrity and on the other --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's not a proper question for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Doyle, in your testimony you mentioned and made reference exclusively to the beginning of arming by the Serbs. This is paragraph 7, page 3, "The Community became aware that a part of population, that is, the Serbs, that the Serbs were beginning to arm themselves." Did you have any knowledge about the arming of the Muslims? Because you make no mention of that, yet you were a monitor. And we saw what was going on.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: During that period when I was head of the monitor mission and before that, when I was a member of the mission itself in Banja Luka, I had visited locations like Doboj, Gracanica, Srbac, Kobas, Derventa, Teslic, Maglaj, and in all of those areas we met with the local Serb leadership, Muslim leadership, and Croat leadership. And in most of the cases the mission was aware of the fact that it was the Serb community that were being mostly armed by weapons been given to them from the JNA. And this occurred because when President Izetbegovic declared that there should not be a call-up for mobilisation of the citizens of Bosnia, most of the Muslims and the Croats did not come up for mobilisation, whereas the Serbs did. And because the Serbs were mobilised to come up for their approximate two months of military service with the JNA, they were allowed to retain the weapons when they finished that mobilisation. That was the mission's clear understanding. And a consequence of that obviously was that if the Serbs were coming up for mobilisation and being allowed to hold onto their weapons, there was going to be a gradual increase in the amount of weapons that were available to the Serbs. And this was a factor that was repeated in a lot of the opstina that the monitor mission visited at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So the arming of the Muslims and Croats was not of interest to you; is that right? You had no knowledge of that.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had no knowledge of that, and I'm not saying that it was not of interest to me. Of course it was. It was my duty to accurately reflect the role of the monitor mission, which was to observe and report. And this is what we reported.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't notice anywhere in your statement that you make any mention of the other sides to the conflict. Maybe I missed something, Mr. Doyle.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was never an issue for the monitor mission in their reports. There was no allegations, for example, by the Serbs that the Muslims and Croats were arming. Our information at the time and what we could see on the ground indicated to us that it would be very difficult for the Croats and Muslims to get weapons, because they had no means of doing that. I'm not saying that they didn't get some weapons from some sources. But we have no evidence of it and it was never mentioned to us by the Serbs. But it was continuously mentioned to us by the Muslims and the Croats that it was the Serbs that were gaining access to weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say that there is no evidence, yet Lord Owen, as you know, was not involved in any kind of monitoring missions or observing arming or anything like that, but he was a negotiator on behalf of the international community and in his book, "The Balkan Odyssey," on page 146 says, and I quote him, "The picture of the Bosnian Muslims deprived of weapons, the picture, the image of Bosnian Muslims without weapons was not disturbed even when Alija Izetbegovic openly admitted on television that the Bosnian government had, through secret channels, smuggled in weapons." And then he speaks of millions of rounds, mines, rifles, et cetera, not to mention what they seized from the JNA. So this picture of the Bosnian Muslims that were unarmed, that was created by the media throughout, even he says that this picture was false. Do you think that he says so without any foundation?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't generally comment on what Lord Owen may have said. I know he wasn't in the country when I was there, which was 1991, and I'm giving you the evidence of what was known to me at that time from my experience of being in the country and visiting a very large amount of the municipalities. I have no comment on General Owen's [sic] opinion as to what happened. I did say before that I'm not saying that no weapons were given to the Muslims, and there's no question in Lord Owen as to when exactly the weapons were given out. I don't know when it refers to, so I would prefer not to comment on that book. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Doyle. But here is a very specific question: I assume that the Monitoring Mission of the European Community in Yugoslavia and you personally must have known that the Croatian and Muslim groupings - and when I say "Croatian," I'm referring to the regular Croatian army - in the village of Sijekovac near Bosanski Brod committed a massacre against unarmed Serbs on the 26th of March, 1992, when several dozen civilians were killed, and more than 50 houses torched and destroyed, old men, children, et cetera. Surely you know about that as a monitor of the European Community in Yugoslavia. And this was precisely in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina and it took place on the 26th of March, 1992. Did you make a report about that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the 26th of March, I was in Ireland. I had finished my mission in Bosnia as head of the monitor mission, so I have no comment on that. I was not aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When did you come back again, Mr. Doyle?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I returned on the 10th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So 14 days after this massacre, in the surroundings of Bosanski Brod, and you learnt absolutely nothing about it?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I returned on the 10th of April, we immediately went into negotiations with the party leaders, as in my statement. I also mentioned that the monitor mission teams were finding it increasingly difficult to get access to locations where some incidents may have taken place. I made reference, for example, to Zvornik. And it became the practice of the mission not to pass any comment on -- on rumours of what may and may not have occurred unless they had first-hand knowledge of it. So where we were aware that there was a lot of conflict, I cannot make a specific reference to that specific incident because it occurred when I was in Ireland and I was concerned about what was happening on the ground when I was there and my energy was put into that at that stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You have two minutes left, Mr. Milosevic, if you want to ask the witness about something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Since you returned on the 10th, do you know that between the 3rd and 6th of April, 1992, that is, just four days prior to your return, that the army of the Republic of Croatia in Kupres, in Bosnia-Herzegovina, killed 56 Serbs from various locations and took 168 into captivity? Surely you knew about that. It wasn't a negligible incident.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of my work dealt with the Republic of Bosnia. I had no experience at all of what was happening in Croatia. It was not within my remit, so I have no comment on it because I was not aware. I was aware in general terms --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This was in Bosnia. Kupres is in Bosnia, Mr. Doyle.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. I thought --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I am talking about the presence of the regular Croatian army within the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and these events that took place there. Do you know anything about the presence of regular Croatian forces in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina and, therefore, also about this massacre of Serbs only four days prior to your return? And it happened in Kupres. Do you know anything about it?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of the details of that incident. I'm sorry I misinterpreted you. I thought it was within the Republic of Croatia. Yes, I know that Kupres is in Bosnia, but I have no intimate detail of that incident, except being aware that an incident had occurred and that some Serbs were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know anything at all about the presence of regular Croatian forces in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina during your term in the monitoring mission and as an envoy of Lord Carrington?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was of concern to me that there were incidents of soldiers of the Republic of Croatia entering into Western Herzegovina, and that was of concern and was submitted as part of a report I made out to my headquarters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This must be your last question, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Doyle, since I have mentioned some really major incidents here, do you know that on the 15th of May, 1992 in the centre of Tuzla during the evacuation of the remaining members of the JNA and the remaining equipment from their barracks, an ambush, a pre-prepared ambush was staged and the column attacked and people were burning like torches, a real massacre was committed? Do you know that? Did you compile a report about that? Did you react to that?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't my wont to make reports on military incidents that occurred when I was no longer head of the monitor mission. At that time I was Lord Carrington's personal representative, so I'm not familiar with that specific incident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Doyle, I would just like to ask you about the events linked to the period of time when you were in Sarajevo. You arrived in Sarajevo on the 24th of November as head of the monitoring mission for Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And with brief interruptions, so far as I can see from your statement, you stayed in Sarajevo up until the 24th of August, 1992; is that right?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was evacuated from Sarajevo on the 12th of May in 1992, and thereafter I was mainly based in Belgrade. I did return on a few occasions to Sarajevo, but not many.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 55 of your statement to the investigators of the Tribunal, you said roughly the following: "The JNA did not interfere in the referendum. It did not take part in the blockade. And it remained in its barracks throughout." Is that right, more or less?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's more or less correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Major movements from the barracks occurred on the 3rd of May, when what you've already described took place; isn't that right? When the officers and soldiers were killed.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And then in the next paragraph, paragraph 56, you said in the first sentence, "Shooting had started around the town with random shooting to and from the barricades." Does that mean that on the 1st of March -- or, rather, the next day all the parties were already armed obviously when it was possible to have shooting to and from the barricades? So they must have all been armed by then.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: People were certainly armed on that occasion. I don't mean that everybody was armed, but I came across an incident at the Bristol Hotel where shooting was taking place between two sides. So obviously they were armed, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did the JNA interfere at all in that conflict at the barricades?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my knowledge, they did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Then in paragraphs 57 and 58, you go on to say that the JNA assisted you with a convoy to the airport. You even said that, "We had to pass through eight checkpoint or barricades and that at each of them a JNA liaison officer and I had to negotiate our passage." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: A moment ago you were asked but you didn't answer that question, because no one asked you to pay attention to it, because indeed in the statement given by General MacKenzie to the OTP here the following is stated: "There were even reports about attacks by Bosnian Serbs on JNA units which tried to hand in their weapons, ammunition, and military equipment to TO forces in return for their safe departure from Bosnian." Are you aware of any such reports, and is this true?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any such reports. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In that connection, I would just like to ask you one more thing: In paragraphs 13, 14, and 15 of your statement, you speak of the period when you arrived in Yugoslavia, which still existed at the time. This is the period of October 1991. And in paragraph 15, in the last sentence, you say, "The federal army was also becoming very much a Serbian army." You had in mind the way the army acted. You were aware of how the army was acting in Sarajevo. Was the army on anyone's side over there?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware that the -- that the majority of the members of the army were Serbs. The monitor mission opened up contact with the JNA who did not recognise our mission at the start. After I met with General Kukanjac, I went on a tour of the country and I met all of the divisional commanders, and it was after that that the JNA admitted to me that it was a mistake on their part not to make the monitor mission welcome. Thereafter, we set up a liaison team with the federal army when we had frequent contact.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I was actually inquiring, Colonel, regarding the time when you arrived in October, because in paragraph 15 you speak about things from those times and you said then that the army had already become a Serbian army. Is that your opinion on the basis of your own insight, or did you hear this from someone else?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was my opinion on the basis of my own insight.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: As early as October?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I would say it was towards the -- not until sometime after I had taken over as head of the mission, so I would say towards the end of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 70 of your statement, you said that "The European Community recognised Bosnia as a sovereign state on the 7th of April." Of course, that is not at issue, is it? But what I would like to draw your attention to has to do with something that is contained in a statement given by General MacKenzie and it is related to what you testified about yesterday in the examination-in-chief, and it deals with the period when you were in Sarajevo. And he said the following: "Up until the 20th or 21st of April, actions by forces of the Bosnian TO conducted throughout the new state had serious repercussions in Sarajevo. And then he says, "On the 12th of April, or around about that date, it was ordered to the TO that it should block JNA barracks, occupy its arms depots and communications centres, and attack JNA soldiers and their families with the view to chasing them out of Bosnia." He says this in his statement and it refers to the month of April, when you were in Sarajevo. So do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no detailed knowledge of that. You must remember that General MacKenzie commanded a large military organisation in Sarajevo. I was an individual person working for the conference in Yugoslavia, and that's where I contained my work to. So I'm not -- I'm not doubting what he said, but nor can I verify it either.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I understand that. But my question relates to what you spoke about yesterday, and that is your attempt to go to Foca to check out the things with reference to the refugees in the area. So what is mentioned here in General MacKenzie's statement, was that one of the reasons why the JNA could not guarantee your safe passage to the location where the refugees were? Could you explain that to Their Honours, please.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, just a correction. It wasn't me who was attempting to go to Foca. I was aware that there was a team from the monitor mission, of which I was no longer a part, attempting to go to Foca. I have no -- I have no idea as to why the JNA advised the team that they could not get to Foca. All they said was, "We cannot guarantee your safety and security, and therefore you won't have the freedom of movement." Why this took place, I simply don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Then in paragraph 96 of your statement, you said that from May you chaired daily meetings between members of the Presidency, Mr. Abdic, Mr. Kljuc, and General Aksentijevic over the withdrawal of the JNA. And then you said you had the strong impression that the JNA wanted to withdraw from Bosnia. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And then in those negotiations you spoke about the airport, the exchange of prisoners of war, the withdrawal of weapons, and those talks were particularly directed, as you stated, towards achieving a cease-fire agreement.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel, I think I and of course the Chamber in the first place are surely interested in how those talks evolved and what results they produced. I didn't quite understand, and for the benefit of the Chamber, could you comment. General MacKenzie says that he had a meeting with you and Lord Carrington on the 23rd of April. Do you remember whether you had that meeting?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On the 23rd of April, I attended a meeting that -- because I had arranged this meeting to be held at the airport for the visit of Lord Carrington and Joao Pinhiero from Portugal, and I was at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But as General MacKenzie says, and I am sure that the Chamber would find it interesting, if you could explain to them whether you remember that it was read out to you a moment ago, that Philip Morillon and General MacKenzie drew your attention to the fact that the Bosnian Presidency was not ready to respect the cease-fire, that this is something they told you? Do you recollect that?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But I should now like to show you another report which MacKenzie sent Nambiar in New York to the UN on the 22nd of June in 1992. Do you remember -- or did you see that document, which is an official document in which under paragraph 2 it says: "We, like the majority of the people, have the impression that the president --" it doesn't say "Izetbegovic," but obviously he is implied -- "wants a major military intervention to return to him his country and his capital." And then later on it says: "It is a fact that the TO forces had initiated clashes and fired grenades and maybe even artillery projectiles on the main Serbian base south-east of the airport." And finally it says: "Until one side sees a strategic benefit from the cease-fire, the fighting continues." Do you remember seeing that report or not?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're referring to that report as a document that was sent to the United Nations by General MacKenzie through his force commander General Nambiar. I certainly don't have any access to those weapons. I'm not a member of the United Nations. I was not a member of the United Nations then. Therefore, there's no reason why I should have access to that -- to that particular report. The second point is that this was on the 22nd of June in 1992. On the 22nd of June, 1992, I was based in Belgrade. I had been evacuated from Sarajevo, so there's no reason that I would have had access to that report, so I know nothing about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: As I don't have much time, let me end with a few points taken again from General MacKenzie's statement. And they have to do with events in Sarajevo. And I would like to ask you kindly to explain if you know anything about them. In one -- he says at one point that "Sarajevo was frequently the target of fierce shelling. Most of the damage was inflicted by cannons of the Bosnian Serbs located on the hills around Sarajevo, but the local citizenry was not aware of the fact that government forces, the TO, had initiated many incidents." Are you aware of this or not?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware of the fact that one of the consequences of the continuous shelling from the hills around Sarajevo was an attempt by the local citizenry to carry out some acts to try and defend themselves. Now, what exactly they did, where they did it, I have no knowledge. But as I mentioned, I think yesterday, in a conflict of this nature, if there are two sides involved, then obviously both sides will have certain weapons and will carry out certain military actions. So I have no reason to disbelieve what General MacKenzie is referring to. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And let me refer to only two more incidents described by General MacKenzie for you to comment on if you know anything about them, but they occurred in the period when you were there, true one on the 16th of July and the other on the 22nd of July, and you returned to Sarajevo on the 1st of August. But nevertheless, could you comment if you can remember, of course. General MacKenzie describes the first incident and says, "On the 16th of July, the day passed in explanations to a delegation of the International Red Cross as to why it would be crazy for us to defend the Kosevo Hospital. I said that the idea would have a meaning in any other peace mission. But in Sarajevo, as soon as we were to position our men round the hospital, forces of the TO would immediately bring their mortars closer to the building, shoot against the other side, provoke reprisals, and then accuse the Serbs of shelling the hospital. Had the hospital been on the side of the Bosnian Serbs, the Serbs would have done the same." Had you heard of this, this incident or others like it?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not aware of that incident. As I said, at that date, the 16th of July, I was not in Bosnia, so I'm not in a position to verify or deny General MacKenzie's report. I have no reason to dispute it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel, on the 22nd of July, the previous afternoon, two soldiers from the N Company noticed that TO forces were preparing a mortar position 50 metres from the outside edge of the BBR base, the UN base. They informed their commander and lodged a protest. However, as soon as the sun set, the mortars were still there with their crews. Immediately after midnight everyone jumped out of their beds when fire was opened from these mortars. Within one minute, 300 soldiers were in their bunkers, the base was shaking, the projectiles exploded in the kitchen, in the dining room, at the command post. Do you know anything about this incident or not?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know nothing about that incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Just one more thing. It has to do with what you testified about in the examination-in-chief. You said that when you spoke to Karadzic about these events, that he said that a conflict would break out. That is the word you used, I think.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're referring to my question to Radovan Karadzic as to what would happen at the event of independence, yes, that is what he said to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And you understood that to mean a war.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm looking at the clock.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I have four questions, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, perhaps just four questions, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tab 5, please, which is the special report on the assembly meeting of the 24th of January. Page 2 of that, under "Comments," this being a meeting about which you've been asked many questions by the accused. Under "Comments" you say this, "It would appear that the SDS, although agreeing to attend the session, were only there for cosmetic purposes and would only support the referendum on attaining unreasonable concessions." Can you explain for us how you formed the judgement that they were there for cosmetic purposes and would condition consent on unreasonable concessions.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: During my time in that parliament, I met a considerable amount of parliamentarians of all sides. I cannot specifically recall what Serb members of parliament I met, but I was under the distinct impression that there was no way that they were going to support the question of a referendum on independence if they were going to find themselves in a minority overall in the parliament, because they were aware that the majority -- the Serb or the Croats and Muslims would outnumber them numerically. And because they hadn't been to parliament in a long time, because they had left the day-to-day running of parliament, as was mentioned by Mr. Milosevic yesterday, the general feeling was that they were only there to show up, to find out what was going to happen, to object to anything that was going to be put forward, and the arguments that took place for the many hours during that parliamentary debate that was translated to me by my interpreter gave me that distinct impression.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This came from direct face-to-face contact with Bosnian Serb parliamentarians?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tab 12, the record of your conversation with the accused, page -- the fourth sheet of it, which begins with the word "Sarajevo," and includes paragraphs 7 and 8. Before we come to it, my second of two questions -- three questions -- or two questions on this document: You haven't told us, but how well informed or otherwise did the accused appear to you to be about matters in which you had an interest?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I got the distinction impression from meeting with Mr. Milosevic, number one that, he was very well briefed on who I was. He was very complimentary to, as he said himself, "what I had been told by the Serbs that you are doing in Bosnia and that you're a person that could be trusted." So my feeling at that stage was Mr. Milosevic had been well briefed on who I was and what I was attempting to achieve. And the second point is that it was my impression that Mr. Milosevic wanted to send a message to the people that directed me to attend the meeting and that I was just going to report back on what Mr. Milosevic said because part of my instructions were not to get involved in debate. So I was there essentially in my view on a listening brief. And Mr. Milosevic mentioned these points about Serb irregulars in the territory of Bosnia, about doing everything he could to stop the flow of weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Et cetera, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 8, then, has him saying, according to your note, this, "That Belgrade could not halt its supply of humanitarian aid to Bosnian Serbs." And then in brackets there's a reference to clothing, food, tents, and money. Did he specify at all what he meant by "money"?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: My last question, this: His protestations about the illegality of the attack on Sarajevo, a Muslim town, did he say anything about how the funding of the VRS could be affected, could be withdrawn?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. Very well. Nothing else. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Colonel, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give it. You are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, my lord.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, the tabs in the exhibits, we should tidy up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It would seem that the exhibit 515, tabs 13 and 14, 19 to 29 are tapes; tab 11 is a transcript and is therefore given to the witness and is therefore a different position.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: But 13 to 14 and 19 to 29 do not seem to me admissible through this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As Your Honour pleases. The document 19 itself I think is the document whereby he produces his identification, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Quite right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So in my submission, that should be admitted and the others can then be withdrawn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You're quite right. 20 to 29 should be withdrawn, 13 and ask 14. Very well. That will be done, and they can be reproduced in another form by another witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much. We'll adjourn now. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Perhaps if the registrar would come up, please. Twenty minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, if the Court would forgive me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: -- Before the witness is sworn, but there's an important administrative matter that needs to be cleared up. It concerns a filing on the 8th of August which relates to a Rule 92 bis (D) application by the Prosecutor. There are three binders of transcripts and supporting materials. That's only been received by the amici within the last 15 minutes. It had to be withdrawn for technical reasons. And so I'd ask that if time could flow from now, rather than the 8th of August, because we hadn't received it before. I would, however, anticipate dealing with it within seven days, so I'd try and file it by next Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, if you would. This is the Sarajevo material.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: But I'm sure technically you can have the extra time, having been served on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'll do it quicker.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. One other administrative matter. It is my understanding that protective measures have been granted for the witness who will testify following Mr. Kraljevic. And so just for the record effectively that would require an effective change in the witness order. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the testimony of this witness will deal with matters related to page 23 of your Croatia atlas.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Sir, is your name Stipan Kraljevic?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Were you born on the 8th of January, 1937?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: In November of 1995, did you provide a statement to an investigator of the Office of the Prosecutor about your experiences in the area of Ilok during the armed conflict in Croatia in 1991?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I gave a statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And at that time, as part of your statement, did you also provide a number of documents to the investigator of the Office of the Prosecutor that related to the situation in Ilok in 1991 and to the expulsion of persons from Ilok between 1993 and 1995?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: More recently, on the 17th of June of this year, 2003, did you have an opportunity to review that statement and make an addendum?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And did you certify to an officer of the Registry of this Tribunal that the remainder of your statement was true and correct?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time I would offer Mr. Kraljevic's statement, the addendum, and the documents into evidence under Rule 92 bis.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, Prosecution Exhibit 516.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, in 1991, Stipan Kraljevic lived in the predominantly Croat town of Ilok in Croatia. Ilok was part of the Municipality of Vukovar and lies on the banks of the Danube River, close to the town of Backa Palanka in the Republic of Serbia. A number of other villages lie close to Ilok, including Lovas, Bapska, Sarengrad, and Tovarnik. Prior to the start of the armed conflict, the majority of the residents of these villages were Croat. By September 1991, many residents of these villages had sought shelter in Ilok, which was completely surrounded by JNA troops and artillery. Mr. Kraljevic was elected president of a multi-ethnic commission tasked with negotiating a peaceful solution to the crisis with the JNA. On the 7th of October, 1991, when the commission met with Colonel Grahovac, the officer in command of that area, Colonel Grahovac told them that Ilok would be destroyed within two hours if the town did not surrender control to the JNA. The commission returned to Ilok and after discussions, informed the JNA that the residents of Ilok could not agree to their demands. On the 11th of October, 1991, the negotiating commission attended a meeting in the town of Sid with Colonel Grahovac and General Arandjelovic, commander of the JNA's Belgrade Corps. The commission suggested that the residents of Ilok be permitted to hand over their weapons to the local police and requested that the JNA not enter the town of Ilok. The JNA officers gave the members of the commission a written list of conditions for the surrender of Ilok, and General Arandjelovic told them that if the residents of Ilok did not comply with the JNA's demands, his units would level Ilok to the ground. The commission returned to Ilok and decided to hold a public referendum on 13 October 1991. The residents of Ilok and the displaced persons located there were asked to consider two questions: 1, are you in favour of surrendering all weapons and signing an agreement with the JNA; yes or no? And 2, are you in favour of collectively moving away due to the crisis situation; yes or no? Seventy-three per cent of the persons who voted elected to leave Ilok. After further negotiations with the JNA, a large convoy was formed on 17 October 1991 and approximately 8.000 persons, mostly Croats, left Ilok and were escorted by Serb forces to the territory controlled by Croat forces. During the next few years, an additional 1500 persons, mostly Croats, were expelled from Ilok. And if I could impose on the registrar just briefly. If we could show the document that is at tab 8 to the witness. And if the English translation of that could be placed on the ELMO. I apologise. I meant to say tab 6. As usual, Ms. Dicklich has the correct information. This is a document that says: "The following is the text of the first voting slip." And then it lists the two questions, the questions that I have just read out. And it says below the second question: "Indicate the number of persons that are to move." And then below it says: "Constitutive part of the referendum was also the text of the agreement, as ultimately given by the JNA represented by General Arandjelovic on the 11th of October, 1991."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
