utterances.text: Mr. Kraljevic, was this one of the documents that you provided to the investigator from the OTP?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And does this document correctly show the questions -- the referendum questions that were provided to the residents of Ilok on the 13th of October, 1991?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you explain to the Trial Chamber, please, why were these two questions presented as the only options for the residents of Ilok at that time.

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for asking. I'll try to explain. The first question was, "Are you in favour of handing over all weapons and signing an agreement with the JNA?" As for that question involved in the referendum, the majority of the population voted no; the reason for it being that in the relations with the JNA until then there was such bad experience. For Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. example, in Tovarnik, Ilaca, Lovas, Bapska, and in other places as well. Wherever the JNA came in, great problems occurred and also the population suffered. So the only hope was to preserve the safety of the town in this way. The second question is: "Are you in favour of collectively moving out due to the crisis situation?" That has to do with the fact that Ilok was surrounded for over a month. There was no electricity in Backa Palanka. It had been cut off. There were constant attacks launched on Ilok, and practically the only possibility for the population was to move out of the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If I can just clarify that. You say that "the only hope was to preserve the safety of the town in this way." By "in this way --" and you were referring to the first question in the referendum. Are you saying that it would have been -- it would have preserved the safety of the town in Ilok by surrendering weapons and signing an agreement with the JNA, or are you saying something different?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: I wish to say the following: There was peace in Ilok. There were no ethnic conflicts. The police maintained law and order and peace, and quite simply we asked that the police continue keeping law and order and peace in town and that the army should not enter town.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. And if the answer to the first question was no, that the army should not enter the town, then why was the next option to collectively move away?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: The second option for a collective move away was due to what I already mentioned, that is, the very bad experience with the Yugoslav army to date in the villages that came under the command of the Yugoslav army. There was a great deal of suffering there, and finally the entire populations were expelled from those particular places.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So what did you and your neighbours fear if the town were surrendered to the JNA?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: We were fearful because this ultimatum of the army said that they had the right to enter any house, to search it, and to punish any person they deemed should be punished.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you. Nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kraljevic, you held political office in Ilok, different offices, and as far as I could see you have a university education; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I assume that you are quite familiar with the situation and that you understood the situation that prevailed in the time that you're testifying about.

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say that the inhabitants of Ilok lived in peace for years with their neighbours, that the town had a mixed population from an ethnic point of view, although the Croats did constitute a majority, and that after the elections in 1990 tensions went up; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Until then for decades there had been no problems; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, we can't put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Could you please explain what you said just now, that we can't put it that way. What kind of problems were there?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, for example, there wasn't a proper equality of rights. The police was predominantly Serb, in terms of ethnic composition. The leadership was of the same ratio in town, although 70 per cent of the population was of the ethnic composition it was. However, the leadership was quite different.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Could you explain to me, when you say "the leadership," I assume that you mean the leadership of the municipality. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who elected the municipal leaders? Was it the citizens who elected the assemblymen, the members of the Municipal Assembly, and did then the Assembly elect its president and its executive council and so on? Wasn't that the way it was?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, in a way, but we all know what elections are like in socialism.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But you did elect your delegates to the Municipal Assembly until then, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: You know, Mr. Milosevic, that there was a one-party system and that everything was done on orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that everything was done on orders. I know that there were always several candidates in the elections and that citizens voted for their representatives and sent them to different echelons of government.

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Theoretically, yes; practically, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you hold an office until 1990?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: I was director of the secondary school until 1973. Then after that, I wasn't anywhere, except that I worked in the secondary school as an agricultural engineer. In 1990, after the multi-party elections, I was only in the local committee of the town of Ilok and I did not have any other authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On the basis of what you're saying, it can be derived that in Ilok, which had a majority Croat population -- actually, was it a municipality at the time?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Until 1963, it was a municipality. And from 1963 until 1993, it was a local commune.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Within the municipality of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Within the municipality of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And who headed this local commune? Was it a Serb or a Croat?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: It was a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know of any Croats who were also in the leadership?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: There were some Croats too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say that Serbs were predominant.

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you said on orders, that this is what was directed.

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, if possible, I wouldn't like to answer any more questions of that nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, since you said that in the police at the time too, that is to say, in the organs of the interior, the majority was Serb, in Yugoslavia did anyone ever order someone to work in the police force or did people apply on their own to attend police school and then to get a job afterwards?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: I have already stated that that's the way it was, and I don't think I should answer any more questions of this nature, because it is well known who appointed the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, people were employed in the police, like anywhere else. As far as I know, it was employment like any other.

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, let the services who were in charge of that testify about that. I was not in charge of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Kraljevic. Tell me, what caused this tension which occurred after the elections of 1990, as you've said?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Before the actual elections in 1990, the multi-party elections, something happened straight away. An allegedly unidentified group destroyed a few monuments at the Orthodox cemetery in Ilok. Actually, they were just turned over. And of course, the press immediately accused the Croats of having done that. However, TV Novi Sad arrived at that cemetery before the police had found out about it, so it was organised. It was staged, in a way. For example, this is how tension was being created. Also, in August 1991, Express Politika, a daily newspaper, carried an article saying that in Ilok 11 civilians were killed and that they were being shown to all by way of a warning for all nationalists. So there was Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. not -- there was no such thing. Nothing like that happened in Ilok. This was all made up, and it only served the purpose of creating tensions. Similarly, it was published in the Belgrade press that, for instance, the Principovac hospital, which is located on the very border between Croatia and Serbia, in fact, part of it is in the territory of Croatia and another part in the territory of Serbia, was a target of an attack by Ustashas who came and mistreated children. It also caused anxiety among the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that there were no incidents at all in the municipality of Vukovar in the time you are talking about? No incidents?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, there were some. For instance, on the 2nd of July, in Borovo, 12 policemen were killed. Also, there were barricades in Trpinje, in Borovo, Negoslavci, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The date, correction, is the 2nd of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said that you were elected at the elections. You remember the changes that happened in Croatia in 1991, changes to the constitution and a series of other events, the new laws that were enacted, et cetera, causing concern to the Serbs. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: I do, in fact. I know that a large part of the police force, policemen of Serb ethnicity, reacted to the decision that the red star, which was the emblem until then, should be replaced by the Croatian flag by leaving their jobs and going to Backa Palanka to continue to work there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And why did the policemen react to the chequer-board flag?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: You call it the chequer-board flag, and we call it the state coat of arms. I don't know, Mr. Milosevic, why they reacted. Those policemen who remained in Ilok continued in their work as usual, although they were of Serb ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know with regard to these constitutional amendments that Serbs no longer had the status of an equal people in Croatia and that a series of new laws were enacted? I enumerated them here before. I have no time to do it again. I know you are aware of them, being an educated man. Do you know that they, among other things, were the reasons for this anxiety and do you know that they were subject to various sorts of pressure?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: There were no pressures in Ilok, although I am aware that certain people of Serb ethnicity went overnight to Backa Palanka and returned in the day. But nothing happened to anyone at night or day, and the property that was left behind was not damaged at all. It was preserved like any other property.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: For those who are not aware of it, Backa Palanka is right across the bridge.

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: That's correct. They have regular intercity communications and there were two busses, one belonging to Backa Palanka, another to Ilok, and the traffic between the two places was normal via these intercity busses. One day, some people intercepted the bus in Backa Palanka, the bus was taken and given to Dunav Prijebus [phoen], a haulier's enterprise, and it was practically stolen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you believe at the time when all this was going on - I also mean the constitutional changes and the new laws - did you believe that discrimination existed against the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: It is my opinion there was no discrimination. There was an aspiration to establish equality among all the citizens in the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How do you think equality was established by excluding Serbs as a people from the constitution of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that this happened at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Until then, Croatia was a state of the Croatian, Serbian peoples, and other citizens. Under the new constitution, Serbs were eliminated as a nation.

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: I would not like to discuss legal enactments. I would leave it to the experts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. These changes, without going into finer points of law, do you believe that the chequer-board flag might have reminded Serbs of Ustasha symbols from the Second World War?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what it reminded Serbs of, but the Croatian coat of arms is an old one and it is not an Ustasha symbol.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You can argue about it being an old symbol, but you know the sufferings Serbs had gone through under that coat of arms in the Second World War.

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: I believe I am giving evidence about the year 1991, and I don't believe this trial is about 1941-1945.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We've been through this. This is a complete waste of time. Let's move on to more recent events.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please: Since you say in paragraph 6, "Under the 1994 constitution, every city, every town had the right to form their own TO units up to 500 men."

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You rejected that constitution by amending it; is that so?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: After the proclamation of independence by Croatia, did the town of Ilok set up units of civilian defence that were linked up with the police, as you say in paragraph 6 of your statement?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that the Croatia police then armed these men?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: The weaponry of the Territorial Defence that was planned to be used by Ilok was confiscated by the Yugoslav People's Army -- had been confiscated by the Yugoslav People's Army earlier, so the weaponry that was available consisted of several automatic rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Why was the civilian defence unit armed?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: To maintain order in the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was there any disturbance in town so that civilian defence needed to be engaged, in addition to regular police?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Army troops came to the border and wanted to enter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: At the time which you are testifying about, the army was the legal Yugoslav People's Army deployed throughout the territory of the former SFRY.

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, whatever you say. Let it be your opinion. You don't believe that it was the legal armed force of the SFRY at the time.

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: It did not treat everyone equally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that there were mass layoffs of Serbs in Croatia mostly in the police force but also Croats who were deemed unfit, not only Serbs?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: If we are talk about Ilok, this didn't happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So all the Serbs who worked in the Ilok police force remained to work there?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. At least, I have no information to the contrary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, then. Were there any problems regarding the Territorial Defence before in the territory of Ilok during the maspok movement in the '70s?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: I'd rather not discuss that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: I know that there was political turmoil at the time, but I don't know what happened with the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was it also a time when there were attempts to establish within the TO some sort of youth units?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Why was it, then, that President Tito replaced the Croatian leadership at the time?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Again, I must say I wouldn't like to discuss that. I don't know anything about it. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Twenty years before the events we are dealing with are quite irrelevant. Move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You say that the JNA took over the weapons from the depots of the Territorial Defence; is that so?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that this decision for the army to take over the weaponry of the Territorial Defence applied to all of Yugoslavia, to all republics?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: I think - and I said this before - that the Yugoslav People's Army did not treat all republics or all parts of our state equally. So I don't know whether TO weapons were seized in Serbia, Bosnia, Slovenia, or other parts of the country, but I know it happened in Ilok.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It was not a question of seizing. It was a decision of the Presidency of the SFRY that the army should take under its control the weaponry of the TO in all republics.

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: All I know is that the JNA armed also the Serbian citizenry, which is not according to the constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did the army arm the Serbs in Ilok perhaps? Do you know that the army armed the Serbs in Ilok?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that for a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You say that in July the JNA shelled Ilok.

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Without any provocation whatsoever on the 25th of May Bridge.

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Isn't quite the opposite true, that one tank was then destroyed while crossing the bridge, the tank belonged to the JNA and it was destroyed certainly by somebody who did not belong to the JNA?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: This is what the event was like: The checkpoint of the Yugoslav People's Army was located on the Ilok side of the bridge, where a police checkpoint used to be. And at a distance of perhaps 200 metres there were JNA men and the police of the town of Ilok. Suddenly a vehicle of the police administration of Ilok was destroyed by artillery weapons. One policeman was killed and three were wounded. There were four men in total. The police vehicle burnt. One policeman who was nearby fired a guided -- I don't know what it's called exactly -- from a hand-held launcher and destroyed that tank, and the crew consisted of six or seven men, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: They were deployed there?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So according to you, was that the reason why the JNA demanded that these weapons be put under their control?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that demand followed immediately. But they wanted these weapons to be put under the control of the JNA, not the Ilok police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But was Ilok supposed to have rocket launchers capable of destroying tanks as part of police weaponry? Is that a proper part of police weaponry?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Do you know that with the beginning of the crisis in 1990 and 1991 the focus of activities related to the secession of Croatia was precisely this war of the -- war against the JNA and its break-up?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: That's what you say. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember the all-out attack on barracks throughout Croatia, the blockades of barracks --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He's giving evidence about Ilok. Now, confine your answers to that or matters that he can deal with, relevant matters. We've heard other evidence about these matters, and there may be other witnesses who can deal with them, but just concentrate on Ilok for this witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. But even what happened on the 8th of July, 1991, on that bridge when that tank was destroyed, that was also one of the attacks against the JNA.

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But before that, as I described, policemen were killed. And the following day, JNA aircraft opened fire from machine-guns on Principovac hospital, also wounded several policemen, and killed one of them. These people were playing football.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please tell me. You said "open machine-gun fire, killing policemen from Ilok." It was before this event; right?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who shot at the policemen?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: The JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know this for a fact?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Nobody else could have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You conclude that nobody else could have shot at the policemen and that's why you ascribe it to the JNA, but you didn't see it with your own eyes.

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Of course I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Why would the JNA shoot at a police vehicle without any provocation, without rhyme or reason?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, that's a matter for the JNA to answer, not for him. Is there any reason -- we can perhaps put it this way: Is it known what reason or was it obvious what reason there might have been for the JNA to shoot at the police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know exactly what the reason was. Until that time, traffic of citizens between Ilok and Backa Palanka had been normal. And when I say "normal," I mean that at all times it was under the supervision of the police but also the JNA. We can only guess at what happened. I wouldn't like to guess. But it is highly probable, in fact 100 per cent certain, that the JNA did this, because they admitted to it. Captain Grahovac admitted that it was they who did it. I know this for a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So what did he cite as a reason, if he said that it was they who shot at the police vehicle? What was the reason? You say you have personal knowledge that he confirmed it.

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: He referred to some sort of incident. I don't know where, and I don't think he mentioned it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So are you saying that because of some incident elsewhere somebody shot at a police vehicle out of the blue?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: There was no previous incident to explain it, but that's what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Since you say that you didn't see it yourself, you only surmised that it could only have been done by the JNA.

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: I am not surmising. It is an admission made by Captain Grahovac and the whole police force knows it to be true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. And do you know -- I have seen many documents about it and also listened to testimony even here, that JNA units until they themselves became the target of attack had the sole role of separating parties at conflict and preventing conflict. Is that true or not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness can only answer in respect of Ilok. Was it your impression in Ilok and the surrounding areas that the JNA were merely there to separate the parties?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. They stated clearly that they wanted to enter Ilok and take control. At all meetings, that was their main motto. So there's no reason to say that they wanted to separate them only.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But, Mr. Kraljevic, a tank was destroyed and the JNA wanted the JNA to enter to put that area under its control and for the weapons to be surrendered; isn't is that so? Wasn't that the sequence of events?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: There were demands before that too, but let's say that that was -- that is so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But let us go on to deal specifically with the things you've said. You said that on the 28th of October the inhabitants of Bapska were given Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. an ultimatum in which it said until they -- unless they surrendered their weapons by 1600 hours -- and I am quoting from what is stated here -- "your village will no longer exist on the map." And this was stated in writing.

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This handwritten paper, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Allegedly it was signed by a major, whose signature is illegible; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Slobodan Barjaktarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you know him? Did you meet that man?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Does such a man exist at all?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Surely he does.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: A major can be in command of a battalion, to say the least. Does this resemble a JNA document? Every company has a typewriter and the possibility of communicating in a decent manner. To me this looks like an ordinary forgery.

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: That document was brought by a worker called Boro Todorovic, I think -- no, sorry, Tomic. I apologise. Tomic. Boro Tomic, who is from Sid, and who was employed in the cooperative farm in Bapska, and he brought this document and handed it to representatives of the local community of Bapska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So even the carrier, the person bringing that message, was not a representative of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: He was not. But later on, that Slobodan, this major, spoke to representatives of the local community because they went to attend a meeting with him the next day, and they also say the same regarding that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What is stated here is not in dispute. What is in dispute is that this could be a JNA document.

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: But he sent it. He admitted to sending it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you know that. The person who signed it?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: I'm told that. I was told that by the persons in the local community to whom it was addressed, because they spoke to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So this document is dated the 28th of September, 1991.

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You know that prior to that, by activities which were in a sense headed by Lord Carrington at the time, an agreement was reached to the effect that all armed activity must cease and that all of us supported this?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we remember that. And that gave us hope that a peaceful settlement would be found for the whole area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And it's stated in that agreement that it was necessary for all to withdraw to a sufficient distance, for all fire to cease, for all paramilitary forces to be disarmed and disbanded, for the reservists of the Croatian National Guard to be demobilised and for units to return to barracks. Do you know that your side did not comply with that agreement?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Our people in Ilok, Sarengrad, Bapska held guard duty only in the town or at the very entrance to the town and nowhere beyond that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. I don't wish to elaborate and expand my questions to anything beyond Ilok, but you as a person who was involved in politics in those days and as an educated man must have known that the agreement was not complied with and that conflicts continued, and Kadijevic himself, who's also from Croatia, wrote to Lord Carrington and warned him of this and this was published in all the media. You remember that?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: I remember everything. But I also know that the army kept advancing and taking control of one place after another. Tovarnik was razed to the ground, then on the 24th Ilica, then there was an attack on Lovas when the army and paramilitary unit entered, they took people out of their houses and 23 men were killed on that occasion. All this was happening around that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you making a distinction between the army and paramilitary units?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And doesn't it seem to you, at least on the basis of the information that you have, that this was not done by the army, by members of the army, but various paramilitary units that were clashing?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, one thing is beyond doubt, that those paramilitary units -- some of them came there under the protection of the army and that the army armed them and that they wore such uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, the reservists had a military uniform all over Yugoslavia. You know that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: That's how they came, wearing uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. But let's go back to this meeting with the JNA. You say that you met with Colonel Grahovac.

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All that was required of you was that you surrender your weapons.

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: To surrender weapons and to deposit them at the bridge where they would be under the supervision of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was this something illogical and unreasonable to ask?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But after that, the army was supposed to enter and establish its control and command there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What would the army command over? They wanted to enter to check whether any weapons remained, whether the weapons had been surrendered, whether the agreement was being carried out, nothing more than that. Is that so or not?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: The police of Ilok was capable of maintaining peace and order, and it was peaceful. There was no need for the army to enter the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did the army without reason consider its competent for seizing weapons that could cause tragedies and that it should make sure that all the weapons were surrendered? Wasn't that its work, its job?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: No, it wasn't. It was the job of the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But all this was happening after the army was attacked and a tank destroyed.

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: The army was not attacked. There was strict prohibition on opening fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Except for the tank on the bridge?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and nothing more than that. Not a single other shot was fired at the Yugoslav army in Ilok.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But throughout Croatia there was.

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but in Ilok there wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And surely they didn't take a position on the basis of a situation in one single town, but the situation throughout Croatia where barracks were blocked and many people killed.

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Talk to others about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Does that fit within that context or not, Ilok was not the central issue.

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Ilok was surrounded, and the closest part of the rest of Croatia was 60 kilometres away, so that there was no danger threatening from Ilok.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I won't ask you about other matters, though I hope you will agree with me that it is difficult to draw out of context a single town. One has to observe the whole situation, and I assume that the army adopted its position on the basis of the overall situation, and I assume you will agree with me in that respect. You remember, for instance - and the whole of Yugoslavia knew about this - when 13 soldiers were massacred in the Karlovac barracks on the 21st of September, 1991. You know what the attitude was towards the army.

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: I must tell you that information hardly reached Ilok because all communication means were destroyed, ranging from the TV transmitter in Tovarnik, Papuk, and all the other localities, so that Ilok was virtually isolated. We didn't even have electricity, power later on, though we could listen transistor radios. We could listen to Belgrade and Novi Sad. 25 Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But you could hear Radio Osijek, surely, and some other local stations.

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: If we had better quality transistor radios, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that on the 1st of November and later Croatian forces staged the all-out attack on Western Slavonia and Maslovina [phoen] and mostly the Serb population was victimised and chased out and there was general chaos at the time? Do you remember that, Mr. Kraljevic?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Let me put it this way: As far as I know, this happened when we went into exile. But I heard many statements by the people of Ilok who remained in Ilok, who stayed behind, and who were told by these refugees that the army simply told them to go into exile and via Banja Luka they went to Backa Palanka and Ilok and that many of them were forced by the army. I'm not claiming that all of them were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The people of Ilok?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: No, the Serb population in Western Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Which army had forced them?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: The Yugoslav army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Kraljevic.

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: This is claimed by many people of Ilok who stayed behind in Ilok. I cannot comment on that in any other way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: To save time, I, too, am unable to comment on that. There's common knowledge about the attack on Western Slavonia, how many people were killed, who carried out the attack, all this is common knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. If you have any questions, ask them, rather than commenting.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say that on the 8th of November, three European monitors arrived in town, and in the next three days another two; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: That was on the 8th and 10th of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I noted down that you said November.

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Not November, but October.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: October. Very well. Yes, yes, October. And among them, there was Hugh Cunningham and Petr Kypr, and what did they report?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: We asked Hugh Cunningham to go and check out the situation in Sarengrad and Bapska. He was given permission by the Yugoslav army to go there, to go to Sarengrad, but not to go to Bapska. In those days, both localities were destroyed and mostly under control. Secondly, on the next day, on the 10th, he went to Lovas. I think this was on the 11th. They came to Ilok on the 10th, but on the 11th they went to Lovas. And then they informed me - me and others, representatives of Ilok - that they had spoken to the new president of the local commune in Lovas, and to put it briefly, I can say the following as regards to what he said: There's a local committee consisting of five members. He is a Serb, as the president; his deputy is again a Serb, and three are honest Croats. He said that in Lovas 50 per cent of the population were of local origin and others had settled there from Lika, that these settlers from Lika, that 80 per cent of them should be expelled. According to this statement, he was completely drunk, but never mind. He also received a list of 21 victims that they had buried in a mass grave, which had been killed by these units the day before.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So this leadership consisted of two Serbs, three Croats, and they were protesting against the behaviour of refugees coming from other parts of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: No, no refuse had come from the Serbian part of Croatia. This was just before Christmas.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, where did these people come from? Why did they go there?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: This was the population that had settled there earlier on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, you mean after the Second World War.

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, I see. Now, tell me, please: Since this seems to me to be quite unbelievable, will you please explain to me. You say that you were present when Mr. Rendulic, your man in Sid, asks General Arandjelovic why some people were killed in Lovas and he answered, "It was revenge for the killing of a JNA soldier and his body being found in a cornfield." Is it possible that you heard such a conversation and that a JNA general would explain that the JNA did this out of revenge?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: No, not that I heard it but there were nine representatives of the town of Ilok at that meeting. This multinational commission, there were two Serbs, two Slovaks and Muslims and others on this commission and all of them heard it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I understand that he interpreted what could have been the reason, but not that the JNA had acted out of revenge.

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: No, the JNA had done it out of revenge.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The JNA? Very well, Mr. Kraljevic. That statement I find quite unbelievable and that's why I wanted to clarify it. You mentioned the referendum, and a moment ago Mr. Saxon asked you about this referendum. However, talking about the voting, do you know that in that area, at those elections of 1990, the majority of Serbs voted for the League of Communists of Croatia, the SDP of Ivica Racan, and that on that list the number of -- a number of Serbs entered the Croatian Assembly, from that list? So the Serbs from the area did not vote for any Serb nationalist parties but they voted for the SKHDSP. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: There were multinational elections. There were several parties, and everyone voted as they wanted to vote. I am familiar with the results of the elections.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are they the ones that I just pointed out to you?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. But I know the results of the election.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The referendum. You explained the questions, and I am not going to lose any time over those questions any longer. Since I do not know except for these documents that were submitted to me, I don't know anything else about your testimony. I read this agreement. I took the agreement and I read it. I got it from the representatives of Mr. Saxon, who put questions to you. "Article 1: On the basis of the request of Ilok, Bapska, and Sarengrad, and after --"

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Could it simply be clarified which agreement Mr. Milosevic is referring to? Because I believe we have more than one document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And the witness should have a copy of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think it's tab 7.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is that right, Mr. Milosevic, tab 7? The agreement refers to Sid --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think so, yes. Yes. Seven, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Make sure the witness has got it before it's put to him. Mr. Kraljevic, I think it's coming up for you. Yes, Mr. Milosevic. Yes, we now have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Article 1 reads as follows -- that's why I don't find what you're saying very clear. How should I put this? You're talking about a kind of behaviour from the JNA that would be quite unacceptable and it doesn't stem from this agreement and that's why I want to have this clarified. I see who the representatives were and I don't have to read all that out and inter alia, you were there too, as a representative of the commission. And then it says, "Based on the request of the residents of Ilok, Bapska, Sarengrad, and after the referendum, all citizens of these settlements as well as the refugees who happened to be in these places can move out if they so wish along with the members of their families." So they can move out. Those who wish to do so can do so, along with the members of their families. And Article 5 says: "Upon the exit of the citizens from the above-mentioned settlements --" and there's a mistake there, a typo, "and before convoys are formed, members of the JNA in the presence of MUP Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. organs and members of the European Community mission will search all objects if there is a need for that." And this is an agreement that was signed in the presence of the representatives of the European Community. The JNA is make it possible for everyone to leave all of those who wish to leave, that is. And then Article 6, please: "JNA members take it upon themselves to ensure the personal property and safety of citizens who will stay behind in these settlements, as well as the property of citizens who used to live in these settlements." So when one reads this agreement, if I understand it correctly, a number of citizens wished to move out, to leave in a safe way. And due to the circumstances involved, they asked the JNA to make this possible for them. They asked the JNA to make it possible for the citizens to do what they wanted to do. And in Article 6 they say they take it upon themselves to guarantee the safety of all of those who wish to remain as well as the property of those who leave and nevertheless leave their property behind. Isn't that right, Mr. Kraljevic?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: We have to be aware of the conditions under which this agreement came into being. First of all, this agreement, when it was signed, the representatives of the international community were there, as is written here. The behaviour of the Yugoslav army was quite different at that point in time. Then at the previous meeting, when there were no representatives of the international community present --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kraljevic --

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's written here that this agreement, when you say here, "On the basis of requests put forth by the residents of Ilok," that was dictated. The citizens of Ilok did not wish to leave. They did not wish to move out. We said quite clearly at that meeting that we did not want the army to enter town. We said that arms would be handed over to the police but that the army should not enter town. However, the army did not agree to that. And we do know what had happened before. I've already said this a few times. In all the places where the army walked in, it was the paramilitaries who also came in under the protection of the army and of course massacres happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, please. So they were not forced to go. They expressed their wish to go from that area.

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: After the war, they returned. So who would move out of his house? You know, wishing to do so. It's really a dubious wish when you have the sword of Damocles hanging over your head.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were conflicts underway?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Wait a moment. Wait a moment. You're both speaking at the same time. We're going to adjourn now. You've got five minutes left, Mr. Milosevic, and then the amici, if there are any questions. Mr. Kraljevic, just a warning we have to give to all witnesses. Don't speak to anybody about your evidence until it's over, please, and that includes the members of the Prosecution team. Twenty minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, may I get a bit more than five minutes? I mean, five minutes is truly not sufficient for me to complete this examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll consider that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You have ten minutes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters cannot hear this, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It says that this is at the request of the residents of Ilok, and it is stated quite explicitly that that was the case that the representatives of the European Community were present, that -- it is also said that citizens who stay, citizens who do not wish to leave, would have their personal safety guaranteed, as was the safety of their personal property. And already in Article 7 it says that, "The organs of the MUP from Ilok, about 60 of them, who possess official weapons will keep these weapons." So they are not even disarming the police. The policemen who were in Ilok will keep their personal weapons and they will go with them and make it possible for them to come. So is it clear from this agreement that this is at the request of citizens, that the army is making it possible for those who -- who wish to leave to leave safely, in view of the great many conflicts that were taking place in the area, that kind of guarantee had to exist; whereas, those who are staying behind will have their safety guaranteed, as well as the safety of their property? Is that right or is that not right?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: After signing this agreement, which was dictated to a great extent -- it was dictated by a lawyer from Sid wearing a military uniform -- we explained to the citizens that those who wished to stay behind can stay behind and that those who wished to leave can leave in a convoy. Then this agreement was signed with the army and the army would guarantee safety, and that is what happened. However, there were other examples as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please, I'm asking you about this now.

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you about this. Is it clear that this was not under any kind of coercion, that this was your wish, just as those who stayed behind wished to stay behind?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, it says in that ultimatum, "The army shall enter town, take over town and exercise control over town," and that's exactly what they did when we left and they would have done it even without that. And of course, there would have been consequences like those that happened in other towns.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We cannot engage in guesswork now, what would have happened had it happened. Let's clarify something else here. You say that they talked to you differently when the representatives of the European Community were not there, but then on this occasion the representatives of the European Community were there, so you could have objected. You could have said, "We wanted to change Article 1 or Article 6, 7, 8," any article, in terms of form and in terms of substance. This is something that constitutes an agreement between two sides.

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we asked that the army not enter town. We said that the police could guarantee safety in town, and this was not allowed. Another matter: What would have happened? What happened happened. We see that those who stayed behind, 1500 people had to leave their homes over these past five years. So it can be seen what the actual purpose of this was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it cannot be seen from this agreement. If you think it can be seen from something else --

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: It can be seen. The army was satisfied to see the population leave and to ethnically cleanse this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On the basis of what do you draw that conclusion, that the army was satisfied if the population left and it is guaranteeing the safety of those who stayed behind?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, they want the population to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So that they would not guarantee their safety, those who stayed behind why would they do that? It is the will of the citizens to leave, not of the army.

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, the guarantee is the kind that was given beforehand. They never abided by it. One thing was said and another thing was being done.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Was this agreement carried out the way it was written here?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did the policemen keep their weapons?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were people safely transported and were they taken over by the Croat police?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I can say that from a political and propaganda point of view this was suitable.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, so it's for a political and propaganda reasons that they did this. All right. It seems to me that we have sufficiently clarified this agreement, then. Please, what does this document mean? I see in the upper right-hand corner it says, "SK2." It is 00366022, that number of yours, list of the victims of the war for the homeland in 1992. Please take a look at this. Not a single person got killed in Ilok.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness have the document, if he can identify it. Mr. Saxon, can you assist us as to which document it is, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I am not sure which document. It may not be a document that is part of this package, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Yes, Mr. Milosevic, what is the question about the document? And then let the witness see it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's this list of the civilian victims of the homeland war until the 17th of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please take a look at this. Not a single person got killed in Ilok here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Have a look. Let the witness see the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Eleven names.

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Let me say this: Frano Dobrinja and Samjuel Fabri were killed in Vukovar. They were in a passenger vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We don't have time for that.

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Nada Vrbanic -- Nada Vrbanic got killed in Bapska. That is the area of Ilok. After this, practically at the time of the signing of the agreement itself, on the 14th of October in Bapska. That's when she was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I just want to have this established. I am showing you this document, and I am telling you that no one here was killed in Ilok, and you are talking about Ilok.

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: I am talking about Ilok.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then I'm asking you about other things, and then you say that you are talking about Ilok. But now I am asking you about Ilok.

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: I am talking about Ilok because Sarengrad, Bapska, Mohovo are within Ilok.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness identify this document. Mr. Kraljevic, what is the document that you've been handed? Yes. Can you tell us what the heading is? Can you tell us what the heading is, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "List of civilian victims of the homeland war." We simply listed the people who got killed during the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is that a document which you yourself produced or were involved in producing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is. I made this while I was mayor-in-exile in 1995. I simply took the personal details down for all the people who made contact with me, including the details of their family who got killed, including the way in which they got killed, without any further ambitions. For instance, Jule Saracevic got killed during the shelling by the JNA of precisely the town of Sarengrad. Miroslav Kolak and Tivic [phoen] got killed precisely when they wished to leave this occupied territory outside of the convoy. And these citizens in the lower part of the list got killed in this way. Many of them wished to leave the location even before the convoy was organised, but instead they were taken to a camp in Begejci, mistreated, and so on and so forth. There is a lot of information. It's difficult to cover it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We've seen this list, but let us look at the following list, which you also introduced. It says, "SK3," "List of victims after the 17th of December." You signed this.

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: I also registered the people who got killed in various ways, in various locations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: I mean only the people who made contact with me or their families.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I see. I understand this. Look at this list, following the list of victims of the homeland war. Under number 2, it says, "Killed outside of his own house." In --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] The witness does not have a copy of this list.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Wait a moment. Let the accused have the question and then the witness can have a look at it. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All I have is this one copy that I received from the associates of Mr. Saxon and I have several questions regarding this document.

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: I know which list you're talking about. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: For instance, you listed the victims of the homeland war. And under number 3 it says, "Suicide." Number 4, "suicide." Number 5, "suicide." You wrote it yourself. Under number 6, you said "died." Number 7, "died in January 1992," and so on.

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Number 9, "Died in Opatija." Then again under number 11, somebody with your last name, Kraljevic, "died." Number 12, "Died in Ilok due to injuries sustained during a burglary." Number 13, again, "died."

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Can I explain?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Then it says one of them died in hospital. And then you have here another suicide, number 32. 34, again suicide; 36, a woman who died around a certain date. Then number 39, "traffic accident." Number 40, "Stepped on a mine." Followed by many other names, "stepped on a mine." Another name, "Died in hospital in Vukovar."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm going to interrupt you to find out what's the point of the question. What do you want to question the witness about?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am asking the witness what victims of the homeland war he's talking about in this list which he signed himself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We have it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because it says here among other things "got killed in a traffic accident."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters cannot hear this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I am stopping this. Let the witness have the document in front of him, and then he'll answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I highlighted most of these names which I read out.

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Number 2, Matisa Sopta, "got killed outside of his house by the JNA, a military patrol." He was killed simply because he had visited his friends on the second day after the departure of the convoy. He only crossed the road. He was a retiree from the JNA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kraljevic, as you will understand, time is rather limited. The point that's being made is that some people are being listed as suicide and traffic accident and they're listed under "Victims of the war." And what I think is being suggested is that they can't be victims of the war if they're in that position, if they were killed in traffic accidents or suicide. Perhaps you could clarify that for us, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Milosevic has read out only names where it says "suicide." He only read the word "suicide." But before that word, there is the word "mistreatment." I would not like to comment further upon this. In most cases, people had been mistreated, and even this case involving a traffic accident, the reason for the accident was never established. You have all sorts of traffic accidents. I don't know what exactly happened in this specific case. But in most cases listed here people were killed. For instance, "Zoran Urban, killed at night in the Matija Gubac Street." He was not killed by the JNA but he was killed during the occupation of Ilok and various killings happened during that time, because law and order were not maintained at the time and that's why a huge number of people left, moved out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Do you want -- do you want those two lists exhibited, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, since --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. They will be exhibited and given the next two numbers, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Defence Exhibit 175, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Kraljevic, can I ask you: Are you saying that even in the cases of traffic accidents, that those persons were mistreated by the JNA prior to their traffic accidents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is only one traffic accident or maybe two on this list. I don't think either of them is -- involves any mistreatment by the JNA. But they may be victims in some other way. What I mean to say specifically, this does not involve the JNA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: One more question, Mr. Milosevic, because your time is well and truly up.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let me just ask you a couple of things about the documents that you produced. For instance, under number "SK4," you are providing a list of people who stayed in Ilok after 17 October 1991 but were expelled. Tell me, where were they expelled and who expelled them?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: The pressure on people by the police of Krajina, who was in power in Ilok, was constant, but there was also pressure by individual citizens.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You have a list of people expelled in 1995. Who expelled them in 1995?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: In 1995, particularly after the entry into Ilok of these refugees from the area of Knin and other parts, there was enormous pressure on the citizens still remaining.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would kindly ask Mr. Kraljevic to provide some more explanations about his statement given on the 8th of November, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said, Mr. Kraljevic, on page 4 that the total population of Ilok at that time was 6.797. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: The number of residents, yes, according to the 1991 census, was 6.797.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Then in paragraph 6 you said in June 1991, "Units were always affiliated -- TO units were always affiliated to the JNA." But you say, "After the proclamation of independence in June, the town of Ilok formed a Civilian Defence Force which was affiliated to the police." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know where this passage is exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 6. In B/C/S, it's page 2, second paragraph from below.

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: "Units of the civilian protection of Ilok consisted of up to 500 men."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'll ask you about that later. But you said further down that the town of Ilok, following the proclamation of independence in June formed a Civilian Defence Force which was affiliated to the police. Is that written here?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now, the last sentence: "The unit of the Ilok Civilian Defence consisted of about 200 men. They were armed by the police and financed by local donations. Their weapons were mainly rifles and later on they procured five grenade launchers. Their commander was Josip Vuletic." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now, tell me only one thing: Why in the month of June, that is, immediately after the proclamation of independence, with no conflict around, was it necessary to arm 200 men out of the total of 6.997 population with rifles and grenade launchers?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't think it was exactly as it's written here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: That's what you stated.

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: There were about 30 men, but in June they had only perhaps several rifles. The rest of the equipment, the weaponry, was procured later. Apart from that, there were those events on the bridge and they preceded this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm quoting your words, when you were speaking about the June of 1991 and 200 men being armed with rifles.

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: That is not correct. There were not that many rifles then.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But if we look at tab 2 now, speaking about that ultimatum. And it is addressed to the residents of Bapska village. In the first sentence, tab 2 of the document, it says: "For some time now, JNA units stationed in the municipality of Vukovar have been subjected to attacks by members of the home guard -- National Guard Corps, the Croatian MUP, and armed civilians." Is this correct? Because you've said that they had put an ultimatum, in a certain sense. But is this first sentence correct? Is it true that there were incidents like this, that armed civilians attacked JNA units?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: That is written by this JNA major, no one else. He is stating his opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: That's how I understood it myself. But you said in paragraph 15 of your statement, and you testified to it a moment ago, that you were willing to turn over your weapons to the police, because it is the police's task to maintain law and order. It says here: "We were not ready to turn over our weapons to the JNA."

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So you were not prepared -- you were prepared to give your weapons to the police, who gave you those weapons in the first place, and not the JNA.

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now, answer only a couple of more questions relating to the document under tab 6. You did not wish to surrender your weapons to the JNA and you decided to leave this territory instead.

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: The weaponry was at the end of the day surrendered to the JNA. When we were leaving, we turned over our weapons to the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You didn't mention it a single time until this moment.

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: It's written in the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But did you really do it?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Kraljevic, during his cross-examination, Mr. Milosevic asked whether you and your fellow citizens were forced to go when the convoy left Ilok on the 17th of October. And you responded and made a reference to a sword of Damocles hang over your head. First of all, did you leave as well on the 17th of October in that convoy? Did you leave Ilok on that day?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did you feel you had any choice?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: I felt I had no choice.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic showed you the document that was at tab 9, which is a list of people who were expelled from the Ilok area during 1993. Did you create that list?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You mentioned that pressure was put on people who remained in Ilok. What kind of pressure was put on people so that they felt compelled to leave? Can you be more specific?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: As soon as our convoy left Ilok, army troops entered. But the police also organised themselves. I believe that in effect only one policeman remained in Ilok. Many citizens were taken into custody to police headquarters, to the basement of the police headquarters, and mistreated. Many residents were forced to look where mines were located. They were abused. It was indeed atrocious suffering for individuals, and many people were also stigmatised. Fingers were constantly pointed at people, saying that they belonged to the HDZ, that they were hiding weapons, and it happened all over the place, in Sarengrad, in Bapska village, but also in our town, in Ilok.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did Serb refugees from other parts of the region come to Ilok after 1991?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: The arrival of refugees from other parts of the country started around Christmas of 1991. A little before that, some refugees had come from Vukovar and they settled in empty homes and sometimes in homes that were already inhabited by Croats and were then expelled.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So did the arrival of Serb refugees in Ilok increase the pressure on persons who had stayed in the town?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you. Nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kraljevic, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give it. You are now free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honours, the next witness is a protected witness. It's the witness C-1175, and some arrangements have to be made.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [redacted]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Could we have the current designation repeated. Could you repeat it for us, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It's C-1175.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Sir, please have a look at the sheet of paper in front of you, the pseudonym sheet, and is -- in the first line, is this your name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1175
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In these proceedings, you will be referred to by the number C-1175. Your request for protective measures has been granted. Witness, did you give a statement to an investigator of the Office of the Prosecutor in the year 2001?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1175
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In a subsequent session with this same investigator, were you shown photos from which you identified a glazier and amateur photographer that you knew from Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1175
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you review this statement and its supplement in the presence of a court officer in June of this year and confirm its correctness except for one correction?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1175
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution would like to tender the 92 bis package for the witness, including two sketches and a photo that were actually used during the interviews and referred to in the statements.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 517, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would now like to read a summary of the witness's evidence and just ask very few additional questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness C-1175 is of Serb ethnicity. In 1991 during the events the witness lived in Dalj. End of August, beginning of September 1991, for a period of three weeks the witness served in the Territorial Defence of Dalj and was assigned to the Territorial Defence headquarters. After that, after he left the TO, he used to visit the TO headquarters frequently. The TO headquarters was situated in the building of the local community. The TO commander at that time was Pavle Milanovic, aka Pajo, a certain Milorad Stricevic, who called himself Colonel, was in charge of a the TO security and led a police unit. He resided in a building behind the local community building. The witness observed that Zeljko Raznjatovic, aka Arkan visited both Milanovic and Stricevic. He also saw Radovan Stojcevic, known as Badza and a certain Zavisic come to the TO headquarters. The witness provided a sketch of the layout of the local community building.
